[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Portrait_of_David_Starr_Jordan.jpg/250px-Portrait_of_David_Starr_Jordan.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_David_Starr_Jordan.jpg)

Ichthyologist and founding president of Stanford, [David Starr Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Starr_Jordan "David Starr Jordan")

From an architectural perspective, the Stanfords sought to distinguish their university by emulating the style of English university buildings while also incorporating elements of local [Mission Revival architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Revival_architecture "Mission Revival architecture") and Californian heritage. They specified in the founding grant that the buildings should "be like the old adobe houses of the early Spanish days; they will be one-storied; they will have deep window seats and open fireplaces, and the roofs will be covered with the familiar dark red tiles."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-46) The Stanfords also hired renowned landscape architect [Frederick Law Olmsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Law_Olmsted "Frederick Law Olmsted"), who previously designed the Cornell campus, to design the Stanford campus.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-47)

When [Leland Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leland_Stanford "Leland Stanford") died in 1893, the continued existence of the university was put in jeopardy due to a federal lawsuit against his estate, but [Jane Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Stanford "Jane Stanford") insisted the university remain in operation throughout the financial crisis.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-:5-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-49) The university suffered major damage from the [1906 San Francisco earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_San_Francisco_earthquake "1906 San Francisco earthquake"); most of the damage was repaired, but a new library and gymnasium were demolished, and some original features of [Memorial Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Memorial_Church "Stanford Memorial Church") and the [Quad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Quad_(Stanford_University) "Main Quad (Stanford University)") were never restored.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-50) During the early-20th century, the university added four professional graduate schools. [Stanford University School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_School_of_Medicine "Stanford University School of Medicine") was established in 1908 when the university acquired [Cooper Medical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_Medical_College "Cooper Medical College") in San Francisco;[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-51) it moved to the Stanford campus in 1959.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-52)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/William_Shockley%2C_Stanford_University.jpg/250px-William_Shockley%2C_Stanford_University.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_Shockley,_Stanford_University.jpg)

[William Shockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shockley "William Shockley"), Stanford professor, Nobel laureate in physics, "Father of Silicon Valley"

The university's law department, established as an undergraduate curriculum in 1893, was transitioned into a professional [law school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Law_School "Stanford Law School") starting in 1908 and received accreditation from the [American Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association") in 1923.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-53) The [Stanford University Graduate School of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_Graduate_School_of_Education "Stanford University Graduate School of Education") grew out of the Department of the History and Art of Education, one of the original twenty-one departments at Stanford, and became a professional graduate school in 1917.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-54) The [Stanford Graduate School of Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Graduate_School_of_Business "Stanford Graduate School of Business") was founded in 1925 at the urging of then-trustee [Herbert Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover "Herbert Hoover").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-55) In 1919, [The Hoover Institution on War, Revolution and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Institution "Hoover Institution") was started by [Herbert Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover "Herbert Hoover") to preserve artifacts related to [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). The [SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLAC_National_Accelerator_Laboratory "SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory"), established in 1962, performs research in particle physics.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-56)

In the 1940s and 1950s, [Frederick Terman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Terman "Frederick Terman"), an engineering professor who later became provost, encouraged Stanford engineering graduates to start their own companies and invent products.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-MSV49,50-57) During the 1950s, he established [Stanford Industrial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Industrial_Park "Stanford Industrial Park"), a high-tech commercial campus on university land.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-wipo-58) Also in the 1950s, [William Shockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shockley "William Shockley"), co-inventor of the silicon transistor, recipient of the 1956 [Nobel Prize for Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_for_Physics "Nobel Prize for Physics"), and later professor of physics at Stanford, moved to the Palo Alto area and founded a company, [Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shockley_Semiconductor_Laboratory "Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory"). The next year, [eight of his employees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight") resigned and formed a competing company, [Fairchild Semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor"). The presence of so many high-tech and semiconductor firms helped to establish Stanford and the mid-[Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Peninsula "San Francisco Peninsula") as a hotbed of innovation, eventually named [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley") after the key ingredient in transistors.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-59) Shockley and Terman are both often described as the "fathers of Silicon Valley".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-61)

In the 1950s, [Stanford intentionally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_and_antisemitism#Stanford "Universities and antisemitism") reduced and restricted Jewish admissions, and for decades, denied and dismissed claims from students, parents, and alumni that they were doing so.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-62) Stanford issued its first institutional apology to the Jewish community in 2022 after an internal task force confirmed that the university deliberately discriminated against Jewish applicants, while also misleading those who expressed concerns, including students, parents, alumni, and the [ADL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Defamation_League "Anti-Defamation League").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-63)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-64) Stanford was once considered a school for "the wealthy",[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-65) but controversies in later decades damaged its reputation. The 1971 [Stanford prison experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_prison_experiment "Stanford prison experiment") was criticized as unethical,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-66) and the misuse of government funds from 1981 resulted in severe penalties for the school's research funding,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Los_Angeles_Times-68) and the resignation of President [Donald Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Kennedy "Donald Kennedy") in 1992.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-articles.baltimoresun.com-69)

In the 1960s, Stanford rose from a regional university to one of the most prestigious in the United States, "when it appeared on lists of the "top ten" universities in America... This swift rise to performance [was] understood at the time as related directly to the university's defense contracts..."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-70) Stanford's continues to have a relationship with the defense industry. They currently run a 'Hacking for Defense' class, in which students partner with military companies on national security problems sponsored by the Department of Defense[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-71). In 2021, they opened the Gordian Knot Centre, a hub for national security problems and defense technology programs[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-72). With initial funding of $1.28 million from the U.S. Office of Naval Research, its aim is to, "bridge silos across the Department of Defense (DoD), industry and academia"[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-73).

[Wallace Sterling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Sterling "Wallace Sterling") was the President from 1949 to 1968 and he oversaw the growth of Stanford from a financially troubled regional university to a financially sound, internationally recognized academic powerhouse, "the Harvard of the West".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74) Achievements during Sterling's tenure included:

*   Moving the [Stanford Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Medical_School "Stanford Medical School") from a small, inadequate campus in San Francisco to a new facility on the Stanford campus which was fully integrated into the university to an unusual degree for medical schools.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74)
*   Establishing the Stanford Industrial Park (now the [Stanford Research Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Research_Park "Stanford Research Park")) and the Stanford Shopping Center on leased University land, thus stabilizing the university's finances. The Stanford Industrial Park, together with the university's aggressive pursuit of government research grants, helped to spur the development of [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74)
*   Increasing the number of students receiving financial aid from less than 5% when he took office to more than one-third when he retired.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74)
*   Increasing the size of the student body from 8,300 to 11,300 and the size of the tenured faculty from 322 to 974.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74)
*   Launching the PACE fundraising program, the largest such program ever undertaken by any university up to that time.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74)
*   Launching a building boom on campus that included a new bookstore, post office, student union, dormitories, a faculty club, and many academic buildings.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74)
*   Creating the Overseas Campus program for undergraduates in 1958.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Roxanne-74)

In 2026, the university was declared an [undesirable organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_undesirable_organizations_law "Russian undesirable organizations law") in Russia.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-75)

## Land

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Land")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/View_Stanford.jpg/250px-View_Stanford.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:View_Stanford.jpg)

The center of the campus

Most of Stanford is on an 8,180-acre (12.8 sq mi; 33.1 km 2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-facts-4) campus, one of the largest in the United States.[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-noteLargest-78) It is on the [San Francisco Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Peninsula "San Francisco Peninsula"), in the northwest part of the [Santa Clara Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Clara_Valley "Santa Clara Valley") ([Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley")) approximately 37 miles (60 km) southeast of [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") and approximately 20 miles (30 km) northwest of [San Jose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose,_California "San Jose, California"). Stanford received $4.5 billion in 2006 and spent more than $2.1 billion in Santa Clara and San Mateo counties. In 2008, 60% of this land remained undeveloped.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-79)

Stanford's main campus includes a [census-designated place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford,_California "Stanford, California") within [unincorporated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unincorporated_area "Unincorporated area")[Santa Clara County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Clara_County,_California "Santa Clara County, California"),[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-80) although some of the university land (such as the [Stanford Shopping Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Shopping_Center "Stanford Shopping Center") and the [Stanford Research Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Research_Park "Stanford Research Park")) is within the city limits of [Palo Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California"). The campus also includes much land in unincorporated [San Mateo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Mateo_County,_California "San Mateo County, California") (including the [SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLAC_National_Accelerator_Laboratory "SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory") and the [Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasper_Ridge_Biological_Preserve "Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve")), as well as within the city limits of [Menlo Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menlo_Park,_California "Menlo Park, California") (Stanford Hills neighborhood), [Woodside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodside,_California "Woodside, California"), and [Portola Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portola_Valley,_California "Portola Valley, California").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-stanford_facts_lands-81)

The central campus includes a seasonal lake ([Lake Lagunita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Lagunita "Lake Lagunita"), an irrigation reservoir), home to the vulnerable [California tiger salamander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_tiger_salamander "California tiger salamander"). As of 2012, [Lake Lagunita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Lagunita "Lake Lagunita") was often dry and the university had no plans to artificially fill it.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-82) Heavy rains in January 2023 refilled Lake Lagunita to up to 8 feet of depth.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-83) Two other reservoirs, [Searsville Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Searsville_Lake "Searsville Lake") on [San Francisquito Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisquito_Creek "San Francisquito Creek") and Felt Lake,[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-84) are on more remote sections of the founding grant.

### Non-central campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Non-central campus")]

On the founding grant:

*   [Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasper_Ridge_Biological_Preserve "Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve") is a 1,200-acre (490 ha) natural reserve west of the central campus owned by the university and used by wildlife biologists for research. Researchers and students are involved in biological research. Professors can teach the importance of biological research to the biological community. The primary goal is to understand the system of the natural Earth.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-86)
*   [SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLAC_National_Accelerator_Laboratory "SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory") is a facility west of the central campus operated by the university for the Department of Energy. It contains the longest [linear particle accelerator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_particle_accelerator "Linear particle accelerator") in the world, 2 miles (3.2 km) on a 426-acre (172 ha) area of land.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-87)

Off the founding grant:

*   [Hopkins Marine Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins_Marine_Station "Hopkins Marine Station"), in [Pacific Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Grove,_California "Pacific Grove, California"), California, is a [marine biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_biology "Marine biology") research center owned by the university since 1892. Based on US Pacific Coast, it is one of the oldest marine laboratories. It includes 10 [research laboratories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_laboratories "Research laboratories") and is also used for archaeological exploration purposes.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-88) A graduate student of the anthropology department discovered evidence that the location was home to a Chinese American fishing village in the early 1900s.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-89)
*   Study abroad locations: unlike typical [study abroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_exchange_program "Student exchange program") programs, Stanford itself operates in several locations around the world; thus, each location has Stanford faculty-in-residence and staff in addition to students, creating a "mini-Stanford".[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-90)
*   Redwood City campus, for outpatient medical clinic facilities and many of the university's administrative offices in [Redwood City, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redwood_City,_California "Redwood City, California"), a few miles north of the main campus. In 2005, the university purchased a small, 35-acre (14 ha) campus in Midpoint Technology Park intended for staff offices; development was delayed by the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-91)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-92) In 2015, the university announced a development plan,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-redwood-dec2015-93) and the Redwood City campus opened in March 2019.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-94)
*   The Bass Center in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") provides a base, including housing, for the Stanford in Washington program for undergraduates.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-95) It includes a small art gallery open to the public.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-96)
*   China: Stanford Center at Peking University, housed in the Lee Jung Sen Building, is a small center for researchers and students in collaboration with [Peking University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_University "Peking University").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-pekingcenter-97)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-LeeJung-98)

### Faculty residences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Faculty residences")]

Many Stanford faculty members live in the "Faculty Ghetto", within walking or biking distance of campus.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-99) The Faculty Ghetto is composed of land owned by Stanford. Similar to a [condominium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condominium_(living_space) "Condominium (living space)"), the houses can be bought and sold to other Stanford faculty but the land under the houses is leased for 51 years with the possibility of extensions. Houses in the "Ghetto" appreciate and depreciate, but not as rapidly as overall [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley") values.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-100)

### Other uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Other uses")]

Some of the land is managed to provide revenue for the university such as the [Stanford Shopping Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Shopping_Center "Stanford Shopping Center") and the [Stanford Research Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Research_Park "Stanford Research Park"). Stanford land is also leased for a token rent by the [Palo Alto Unified School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto_Unified_School_District "Palo Alto Unified School District") for several schools including [Palo Alto High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto_High_School "Palo Alto High School") and [Gunn High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunn_High_School "Gunn High School").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-101) El Camino Park, the oldest Palo Alto city park, is also on Stanford land.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-102) Stanford also has the Stanford Golf Course,[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-103) and Stanford Red Barn Equestrian Center,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-104) used by Stanford athletics though the golf course can also be used by the general public.

## Administration and organization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Administration and organization")]

Stanford is a private, non-profit university administered as a [corporate trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_trust "Corporate trust") governed by a privately appointed [board of trustees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_trustees "Board of trustees") with a maximum membership of 38.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-stanford_facts_admin-109)[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-noteTrustees-112) Trustees serve five-year terms (not more than two consecutive terms) and meet five times annually.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-113) A new trustee is chosen by the current trustees by ballot.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-FoundingGrant-110) The Stanford trustees also oversee the [Stanford Research Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Research_Park "Stanford Research Park"), the [Stanford Shopping Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Shopping_Center "Stanford Shopping Center"), the [Cantor Center for Visual Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iris_&_B._Gerald_Cantor_Center_for_Visual_Arts "Iris & B. Gerald Cantor Center for Visual Arts"), [Stanford University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_Medical_Center "Stanford University Medical Center"), and many associated medical facilities (including the [Lucile Packard Children's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucile_Packard_Children's_Hospital "Lucile Packard Children's Hospital")).[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-FG_facts-114)

The board appoints a president to serve as the chief executive officer of the university, to prescribe the duties of professors and course of study, to manage financial and business affairs, and to appoint nine vice presidents.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-115)[Richard Saller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Saller "Richard Saller") became the interim president in September 2023.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-116) On April 4, 2024, the board of trustees announced that [Jonathan Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Levin_(economist) "Jonathan Levin (economist)") would become the thirteenth president on August 1, 2024.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-117) The provost is the chief academic and budget officer, to whom the deans of each of the seven schools report.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-aboutprovost-118)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-119)[Jenny Martinez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jenny_Martinez "Jenny Martinez") became the fourteenth provost in October 2023.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-120) The university is organized into seven academic schools.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-seven-schools-121)

The schools of [Humanities and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_School_of_Humanities_and_Sciences "Stanford University School of Humanities and Sciences") (twenty-seven departments),[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-bulletin-hs-122)[Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_School_of_Engineering "Stanford University School of Engineering") (nine departments),[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-bulletin-engineering-123) and [Sustainability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Doerr_School_of_Sustainability "Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability") (nine departments)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-124) have both graduate and undergraduate programs while the Schools of [Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Law_School "Stanford Law School"),[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-125)[Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_School_of_Medicine "Stanford University School of Medicine"),[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-126)[Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_Graduate_School_of_Education "Stanford University Graduate School of Education"),[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-127) and [Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Graduate_School_of_Business "Stanford Graduate School of Business")[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-128) have graduate programs only. The powers and authority of the faculty are vested in the Academic Council, which is made up of tenure and non-tenure line faculty, research faculty, senior fellows in some policy centers and institutes, the president of the university, and some other academic administrators.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-academic_council-129) But most matters are handled by the Faculty Senate, made up of 54 elected representatives of the faculty for 2021.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-130)

The Associated Students of Stanford University (ASSU) is the student government for Stanford and all registered students are members. Its elected leadership consists of the Undergraduate Senate elected by the undergraduate students, the Graduate Student Council elected by the graduate students, and the President and Vice President elected as a [ticket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticket_(election) "Ticket (election)") by the entire student body.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-131) Stanford is the beneficiary of a special clause in the [California Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Constitution "California Constitution"), which explicitly exempts Stanford property from taxation so long as the property is used for educational purposes.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-132)

### Endowment, assets, and donations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Endowment, assets, and donations")]

Main article: [Stanford University endowment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_endowment "Stanford University endowment")

Stanford's endowment includes real estate and other investments valued at $36.5 billion as of August 2023,[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-133) and is one of the four [largest academic endowments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_the_United_States_by_endowment "List of colleges and universities in the United States by endowment") in the United States.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-134) The endowment consists of $29.9 billion in a merged pool of assets and $6.6 billion of real estate near the main campus. Stanford is the largest landowner in the Silicon Valley[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-135) Payouts from the endowment covered approximately 22% of university expenses in the 2023 fiscal year.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-2023FinRep-136)

Since inception, the university has been the beneficiary of large donations. The endowment began in 1885, six years before the opening of the university, when Leland Stanford and his wife Jane conveyed approximately $20 million to the university.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-137) The university's pioneering of technology intellectual property transfer created both direct investments and enabled a unique pipeline of mega-donors[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-138) including from alumni-founded companies with [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google") ([Sergey Brin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Brin "Sergey Brin") and [Larry Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Page "Larry Page")), [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") ([Phil Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Knight "Phil Knight")),[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-139)[Hewlett-Packard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard") ([David Packard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Packard "David Packard") and [Bill Hewlett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Hewlett "Bill Hewlett")),[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-140) and [Sun Microsystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Microsystems "Sun Microsystems") ([Vinod Khosla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinod_Turn_the_Lights_Back_Onosla?action=edit&redlink=1 "Vinod Turn the Lights Back Onosla (page does not exist)"))[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-141) as examples. Further, the university's global reputation[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-142) and continued leadership in technology[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-143) has attracted large donations from prominent figures such as the co-founder of [Netscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netscape "Netscape") ([Jim Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_H._Clark "James H. Clark")),[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-144) founder of [SAP SE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAP "SAP") ([Hasso Plattner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasso_Plattner "Hasso Plattner")),[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-145) co-founder of [Andreessen Horowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz") ([Marc Andreessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Andreessen "Marc Andreessen") and [Laura Arillaga-Andreessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Arrillaga-Andreessen "Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen")),[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-146) chairman of [Kleiner Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kleiner_Perkins "Kleiner Perkins") ([John Doerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Doerr "John Doerr") and his wife Ann).[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-147)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Academics")]

### Notable Programs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Notable Programs")]

Stanford University is renowned for its programs in Computer Science, Business, Law, and Medicine. The university's School of Engineering includes a top-ranked Computer Science department, while the Graduate School of Business, Law School, and School of Medicine are consistently ranked among the best in the nation.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Admissions

Stanford is considered by _[US News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.\_News\_&\_World\_Report "U.S. News & World Report")_ to be 'most selective' with an acceptance rate of 3.8%, one of the lowest among US universities. Half of the applicants accepted to Stanford have an [SAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT "SAT") score between 1520 and 1570 or an [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_(test) "ACT (test)") score between 32 and 35, typically with a GPA of 3.94 or higher. Admissions officials consider a student's [grade point average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grading_in_education "Grading in education") to be an important academic factor, with emphasis on an applicant's high school class rank and letters of recommendation.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-154) In terms of non-academic materials as of 2019, Stanford ranks extracurricular activities, talent/ability and character/personal qualities as 'very important' in making first-time, first-year admission decisions, while ranking the interview, whether the applicant is a first-generation university applicant, [legacy preferences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legacy_preferences "Legacy preferences"), volunteer work and work experience as 'considered'.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-:3-151)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-155) Of those students accepted to Stanford's Class of 2026, 1,736 chose to attend, of which 21% were first-generation college students.

Stanford's admission process is [need-blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need-blind_admission "Need-blind admission") for U.S. citizens and permanent residents;[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-156) while it is not need-blind for international students, 64% are on need-based aid, with an average aid package of $31,411.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-CDS-157) In 2012, the university awarded $126 million in need-based financial aid to 3,485 students, with an average aid package of $40,460.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-CDS-157) Eighty percent of students receive some form of financial aid.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-CDS-157) Stanford has a no-loan policy.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-CDS-157) For undergraduates admitted starting in 2015, Stanford waives tuition, room, and board for most families with incomes below $65,000, and most families with incomes below $125,000 are not required to pay tuition; those with incomes up to $150,000 may have tuition significantly reduced.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-FA-158) Seventeen percent of students receive [Pell Grants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_Grant "Pell Grant"),[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-CDS-157) a common measure of low-income students at a college. In 2022, Stanford started its first dual-enrollment computer science program for high school students from low-income communities,[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-SRT-159) as a pilot project which then inspired the founding of the Qualia Global Scholars Program.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-160) Stanford plans to expand the program to include courses in Structured Liberal Education and writing.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-SRT-159)

### Teaching and learning

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Teaching and learning")]

Stanford follows a quarter system with the autumn quarter usually beginning in late September and the spring quarter ending in mid-June.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Carnegie-17) The full-time, four-year undergraduate program has arts and sciences focus with high graduate student coexistence.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Carnegie-17) Stanford is accredited by the [Western Association of Schools and Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Association_of_Schools_and_Colleges "Western Association of Schools and Colleges") with the latest review in 2023.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-161)

### Research centers and institutes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Research centers and institutes")]

Main article: [Stanford University centers and institutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_centers_and_institutes "Stanford University centers and institutes")

Stanford is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-Carnegie-17) The university's research expenditure in fiscal years of 2021/22 was $1.82 billion and the total number of sponsored projects was 7,900.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-162) By 2016, the Office of the Vice Provost and Dean of Research oversaw [eighteen independent laboratories, centers, and institutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University_centers_and_institutes "Stanford University centers and institutes"). [Kathryn Ann Moler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_Moler "Kathryn Moler") is the key person for leading those research centers for choosing problems, faculty members, and students. Funding is also provided for undergraduate and graduate students by those labs, centers, and institutes for collaborative research.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-163) Other Stanford-affiliated institutions include the [SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLAC_National_Accelerator_Laboratory "SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory") (originally the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center), the [Stanford Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Research_Institute "Stanford Research Institute") (an independent institution which originated at the university), the [Hoover Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Institution "Hoover Institution") (a conservative [think tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank")),[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-164) and the [Hasso Plattner Institute of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasso_Plattner_Institute_of_Design "Hasso Plattner Institute of Design") (a multidisciplinary design school in cooperation with the [Hasso Plattner Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasso_Plattner_Institute_for_Digital_Engineering "Hasso Plattner Institute for Digital Engineering") of [University of Potsdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Potsdam "University of Potsdam") that integrates product design, engineering, and business management education).

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Hoover_Tower_Stanford_January_2013.jpg/250px-Hoover_Tower_Stanford_January_2013.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hoover_Tower_Stanford_January_2013.jpg)

Hoover Tower, inspired by the cathedral tower at [Salamanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salamanca "Salamanca") in Spain

Stanford is home to the [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") Research and Education Institute, which grew out of and still contains the Martin Luther King Jr. Papers Project, a collaboration with the [King Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Center_for_Nonviolent_Social_Change "King Center for Nonviolent Social Change") to publish the King papers held by the King Center.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-165) It also runs the [John S. Knight Fellowship for Professional Journalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_S._Knight_Fellowships_for_Professional_Journalists "John S. Knight Fellowships for Professional Journalists") and the Center for Ocean Solutions, which brings together marine science and policy to address challenges facing the ocean. It focuses on five points: climate change, overfishing, coastal development, pollution, and plastics.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-166) Together with [UC Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Berkeley "UC Berkeley") and [UC San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_San_Francisco "UC San Francisco"), Stanford is part of the [Biohub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biohub "Biohub"), a new medical science research center founded in 2016 by a $600 million commitment from Facebook CEO and founder [Mark Zuckerberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Zuckerberg "Mark Zuckerberg") and pediatrician [Priscilla Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priscilla_Chan "Priscilla Chan"). This medical research center is working for designing advanced-level health care units.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-167)

### Arts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stanford_University&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Arts")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Les-bourgeois-de-Calais.jpg/250px-Les-bourgeois-de-Calais.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Les-bourgeois-de-Calais.jpg)

Bronze statues by [Auguste Rodin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Rodin "Auguste Rodin") are scattered throughout the campus, including these _[Burghers of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Burghers\_of\_Calais "The Burghers of Calais")_

Stanford is home to the [Cantor Center for Visual Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iris_&_B._Gerald_Cantor_Center_for_Visual_Arts "Iris & B. Gerald Cantor Center for Visual Arts"), a museum established with the help of art collector [B. Gerald Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._Gerald_Cantor "B. Gerald Cantor"). It today consists of twenty-four galleries, sculpture gardens, terraces, and a courtyard first established in 1891 by Jane and Leland Stanford as a memorial to their only child. The university's collection of works by [Auguste Rodin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Rodin "Auguste Rodin") is among the largest in the world,[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-174) with as many as 200 sculptures at the Cantor Center alone. These include an original bronze cast of _[The Thinker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Thinker "The Thinker")_ granted residence at Stanford by Cantor in 1988, with the university expected to attain full ownership sometime in the future. The Stanford _Thinker_ has been loaned for viewing around the world and features across the university's iconography and culture,[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-175)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-176) including the logo of the _Encyclopedia of Philosophy._

The [Thomas Welton Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Welton_Stanford "Thomas Welton Stanford") Gallery, which was built in 1917, serves as a teaching resource for the Department of Art & Art History as well as an exhibition venue. In 2014, Stanford opened the Anderson Collection, a new museum focused on postwar American art and founded by the donation of 121 works by food service moguls Mary and [Harry Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_W._Anderson "Harry W. Anderson").[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-177)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-178)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-179) There are outdoor art installations throughout the campus, primarily sculptures, but some murals as well. The Papua New Guinea Sculpture Garden near Roble Hall features wood carvings and "[totem poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totem_pole "Totem pole")".

The Stanford music department sponsors many ensembles, including five choirs, the Stanford Symphony Orchestra, [Stanford Taiko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Taiko "Stanford Taiko"), and the Stanford Wind Ensemble. Extracurricular activities include theater groups such as Ram's Head Theatrical Society, the Stanford Improvisors,[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-180) the Stanford Shakespeare Company, and the Stanford Savoyards, a group dedicated to performing the works of [Gilbert and Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_and_Sullivan "Gilbert and Sullivan"). Stanford is also host to [ten _a cappella_ groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Stanford_University_a_cappella_groups "List of Stanford University a cappella groups"), including the [Mendicants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Mendicants "Stanford Mendicants") (Stanford's first),[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-181)[Counterpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Counterpoint "Stanford Counterpoint") (the first all-female group on the [West Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_of_the_United_States "West Coast of the United States")),[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-182)[the Harmonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Harmonics "Stanford Harmonics"), the [Stanford Fleet Street Singers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Fleet_Street_Singers "Stanford Fleet Street Singers"),[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-183)[Talisman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talisman_A_Cappella "Talisman A Cappella"), [Everyday People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Everyday_People "Stanford Everyday People"), [and Raagapella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Raagapella "Stanford Raagapella").[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University#cite_note-184)

**Abraham Lincoln**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln#cite_note-4) (February 12, 1809–April 15, 1865) was the 16th president of the United States, serving from 1861 until [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln "Assassination of Abraham Lincoln") in 1865. He led the United States through the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), defeating the [Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America") and playing a major role in the [abolition of slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_slavery_in_the_United_States "End of slavery in the United States").

Born in [a one-room log cabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln_Birthplace_National_Historical_Park "Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park") in [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), Lincoln was raised on the [frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_frontier "American frontier"). He was [self-educated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autodidacticism "Autodidacticism") and became a lawyer, [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois") state [legislator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_House_of_Representatives "Illinois House of Representatives"), and [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._representative "U.S. representative"). Angered by the [Kansas–Nebraska Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas%E2%80%93Nebraska_Act "Kansas–Nebraska Act") of 1854, which opened the territories to slavery, he became a leader of the new [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"). He reached a national audience in the [1858 Senate campaign debates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln%E2%80%93Douglas_debates "Lincoln–Douglas debates") against [Stephen A. Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_A._Douglas "Stephen A. Douglas"). Lincoln won the [1860 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_United_States_presidential_election "1860 United States presidential election"), becoming the first Republican president. His victory prompted a majority of the slave states to begin [seceding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession_in_the_United_States "Secession in the United States") and form the Confederate States. A month after Lincoln assumed the presidency, Confederate forces [attacked Fort Sumter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Sumter "Battle of Fort Sumter"), starting the Civil War.

As a [moderate Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderate_Republicans_(Reconstruction_era) "Moderate Republicans (Reconstruction era)"), Lincoln had to navigate conflicting political opinions from contentious factions during the war effort. He closely supervised the Union's strategy and tactics, including the selection of generals and the implementation of a [naval blockade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_blockade "Union blockade") of Southern ports. He suspended the writ of _[habeas corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habeas\_corpus "Habeas corpus")_ in April 1861, an action that Chief Justice [Roger Taney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Taney "Roger Taney") found in _[Ex parte Merryman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex\_parte\_Merryman "Ex parte Merryman")_ that only Congress could do, and he averted war with [Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") by defusing the [_Trent_ Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trent_Affair "Trent Affair"). On January 1, 1863, he issued the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation"), which declared the slaves in the states "in rebellion" to be free. On November 19, 1863, he delivered the [Gettysburg Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg_Address "Gettysburg Address"), which became one of the most famous speeches in American history. He promoted the [Thirteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_U.S._Constitution "Thirteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution"), which, in 1865, abolished [chattel slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattel_slavery "Chattel slavery"). Following his [re-election in 1864](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1864_United_States_presidential_election "1864 United States presidential election"), he sought to heal the war-torn nation through [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era").

On April 14, 1865, five days after the [Confederate surrender at Appomattox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Appomattox_Court_House "Battle of Appomattox Court House"), Lincoln was fatally shot by [John Wilkes Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkes_Booth "John Wilkes Booth") at [Ford's Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford's_Theatre "Ford's Theatre") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_County,_D.C. "Washington County, D.C."), becoming the first U.S. president to be assassinated. Lincoln is remembered as a [martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martyr "Martyr") and a national hero for his wartime leadership and for his efforts to preserve the [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetual_Union "Perpetual Union") and abolish slavery. He [is consistently ranked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States#Scholar_survey_summary "Historical rankings of presidents of the United States") in both popular and scholarly polls as among the greatest presidents in [American history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_States "History of the United States").
